results.summary: This project implements a 4-bit digital lock that compares a 4-bit input against the fixed password 1010 using discrete logic gates. When the correct combination is entered, an output goes high to turn on a display showing 'U' for unlocked. An SR latch provides a permanent lock condition: entering 1111 triggers the latch and prevents any future unlocking, even with the correct password. The design is intended for educational purposes and requires external switches, logic gates, a 7-segment display, and optionally an LED for debugging.

This project is a seven-segment display decoder that sequentially displays the letters of the name 'thusith' one by one. It uses a 1 Hz clock to advance through the letters, with a multiplexer select pin and BCD inputs controlling which character is shown. The design is implemented in Wokwi and requires an external 7-segment display connected to the segment outputs. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and no testing details.

This project is a 2-bit ALU built from discrete logic gates that computes four operations (ADD, AND, OR, NOT A) in parallel and selects one based on a 2-bit opcode. The result is displayed on a 7-segment display showing digits 0–3. It takes two 2-bit inputs and a 2-bit operation selector, and uses a 2-to-4 decoder and output selector to route the correct result. The design is intended for educational purposes and requires external DIP switches and a 7-segment display.

This project combines a 4-bit asynchronous hexadecimal up-counter and a programmable logic gate validator in a single tile. The counter increments on each clock rising edge and outputs a 4-bit binary count, while the logic validator evaluates AND, OR, XOR, or NOT functions on two data bits based on two control bits, with optional inversion and enable. Two signal buffers route inputs through delay chains to verify path integrity. The design is intended for educational purposes and requires external components such as a 7-segment decoder, LEDs, DIP switches, and a clock source for testing.

This project implements an 8-bit digital lock that compares an input pattern against a hard-coded master key (10110101) using a bit-matching architecture with inverters and an 8-input AND gate tree. When the correct pattern is entered via an external 8-bit DIP switch, a green LED lights up; otherwise, a red LED indicates failure. The design is purely combinational and requires only the DIP switch and two LEDs with resistors as external hardware. It is intended as an educational demonstration of pattern comparison and logic gates.

This project re-implements the 74181 4-bit ALU with inputs coming from programmable 2-bit and 4-bit registers to work within the pin constraints and demonstrate register operation. It deliberately avoids bidirectional pins and provides outputs for the ALU result, carry, and status flags. The design is educational, showing a step toward understanding basic CPU operation, and can be tested with simple external hardware like DIP switches and LEDs. The documentation notes that arbitrary external hardware can be used.

This project is an 8-bit UART transmitter that converts parallel ASCII data (characters 0x40 to 0x5F) into a standard UART frame using a parallel-in-serial-out shift register architecture. It uses D flip-flops and multiplexers to load data and then shift it out serially with start, stop, and idle bits. The design is intended for educational purposes and requires external DIP switches for input, a 7-segment display for debugging, status LEDs, and a logic analyzer or UART-to-USB converter to verify the serial output.

This project is a 4-bit comparator that compares two 4-bit binary numbers A and B using logic gates to determine if A equals B, A is greater than B, or A is less than B. The result is displayed on a 7-segment display as the letters E, H, or L respectively. The design checks bits from MSB to LSB and uses OR logic to drive the display segments. It requires external switches for the inputs and a 7-segment display for output, and is intended as an educational project.

This project creates a hardware security glitch on a chip that can be detected using certain Trojan detection methods. It outputs VGA signals (R1, G1, B1, VSync, R0, G0, B0, HSync) and has inputs for speed and direction. The design is inspired by a Tiny Tapeout workshop and is intended for hardware security experimentation. Testing requires a main PCB that connects the chip to multiple peripherals and provides ports or jumpers for side-channel analysis.

This project implements an analog-controlled 8-pin multiplexer that selects among eight test circuits based on an input voltage from 0V to 1.8V, with thresholds every 200mV. The test circuits include various ring oscillators (3, 5, 7 inverters), frequency dividers using T flip-flops, and a resistor divider, allowing comprehensive testing of the design. The multiplexer uses only two analog pins: one for control voltage and one for the selected output. Testing requires a laboratory power supply, multimeter, and oscilloscope to measure frequencies and signal characteristics.
